intro: In this college you'll learn how to talk about your family in Dutch: name your relatives, describe visits, talk about marriage, living together and divorce, congratulate people at celebrations, and say who looks like whom.

paragraphs.heading: Welcome — your family in Dutch
paragraphs.text: Welcome to theme fourteen. Its title is [[We bellen iedere dag!]], which means 'We call every day!'. Family is one of the warmest topics in any language, and in the Netherlands your neighbours, your colleagues and other parents at school will often ask about yours. So let's build the words you need. The whole family is [[de familie]]. Your parents are [[de ouders]], with [[de moeder]] for mother and [[de vader]] for father. A brother is [[de broer]] and a sister is [[de zus]]. Your children are [[de kinderen]], a son is [[de zoon]] and a daughter is [[de dochter]]. The grandparents are lovely short words: grandma is [[de oma]] and grandpa is [[de opa]], and a grandchild is [[het kleinkind]]. When you marry, you gain in-laws, like your mother-in-law, [[de schoonmoeder]]. In this college I explain everything in English, but every Dutch word you hear is spoken by a native voice, so you train your ear at the same time. Please say each word out loud after me. A friendly opener you will hear constantly is [[Hoe gaat het met je familie?]], which means 'how is your family doing?'. [[Laten we beginnen!]]

paragraphs.heading: Whose family? Possessives
paragraphs.text: To say who a relative belongs to, Dutch uses possessive words, just like English 'my' and 'your'. 'My' is [[mijn]], so 'my mother' is [[mijn moeder]] and 'my brother' is [[mijn broer]]. The informal 'your' is [[jouw]], often shortened to [[je]] in normal speech, so 'your sister' is [[jouw zus]] or simply [[je zus]]. For 'his' you use [[zijn]], as in 'his father', [[zijn vader]]. For 'her' you use [[haar]], as in 'her daughter', [[haar dochter]]. Now here is one small thing that trips everyone up: the word for 'our'. With most nouns, the de-words, you say [[onze]], for example 'our daughter', [[onze dochter]]. But with het-words you say [[ons]], for example 'our grandchild', [[ons kleinkind]]. Listen to the pair again: [[onze dochter]] but [[ons kleinkind]]. A handy sentence to practise is [[Dit is mijn man en dat is onze zoon.]], 'this is my husband and that is our son.' And remember the warm phrase many people feel deeply: [[Ik mis mijn familie heel erg.]], which means 'I miss my family very much.' If your relatives live far away, that is a sentence worth knowing by heart.

paragraphs.heading: Visiting and calling each other
paragraphs.text: In the Netherlands, family life often happens through visits and phone calls. The word for a visit is [[het bezoek]]. To say someone is coming to visit, you say [[op bezoek komen]], for example [[Mijn zus komt morgen op bezoek.]], 'my sister is coming to visit tomorrow.' If you have people coming tonight, you say [[We krijgen vanavond bezoek.]] A very Dutch, casual way to say 'drop by' is [[langskomen]], so you might ask a friend [[Wanneer kom je weer langs?]], 'when are you coming over again?'. For the phone, there is a useful little word: [[elkaar]], which means 'each other'. You use it for things two people do together. So 'we call each other every day' is exactly our title idea: [[We bellen elkaar iedere dag.]] You will also hear it with prepositions, staying together as one piece, like 'they love each other a lot', [[Ze houden veel van elkaar.]] When you say goodbye after a chat about relatives, a sweet, common closing is [[Doe de groeten aan je familie.]], which means 'give my regards to your family.' Practise these out loud — they make you sound friendly and natural straight away.

paragraphs.heading: Looking like each other
paragraphs.text: Dutch people love commenting on family resemblance, so this is a fun and useful corner of the language. The key verb is [[lijken op]], which means 'to look like' or 'to resemble' someone. Notice that little word [[op]] is glued to the verb — you cannot leave it out. So 'you look like your mother' is [[Je lijkt op je moeder.]], and 'my son looks like his father' is [[Mijn zoon lijkt op zijn vader.]] To make it stronger, add [[sprekend]], which means 'exactly', as in [[Je lijkt sprekend op je vader.]], 'you look exactly like your father.' You can ask someone [[Op wie lijk jij het meest?]], which means 'who do you look like the most?'. And when two people clearly resemble each other, the classic warm exclamation is our theme phrase: [[Wat lijken jullie veel op elkaar!]], meaning 'how much you two look alike!'. There is even a lovely Dutch saying for this: [[De appel valt niet ver van de boom.]], literally 'the apple does not fall far from the tree' — children resemble their parents. Try saying it slowly. These little observations are perfect small talk when someone shows you a family photo.

paragraphs.heading: Marriage, living together, divorce
paragraphs.text: Now the big life events. A marriage is [[het huwelijk]], and the wedding party itself is [[de bruiloft]]. The verb 'to marry' is [[trouwen]], and it takes a fixed preposition: you marry 'with' someone, [[trouwen met]]. So 'my brother is getting married in June' is [[Mijn broer gaat in juni trouwen.]] To talk about a wedding in the past, Dutch uses a special form. Importantly, [[trouwen]] takes [[zijn]], not [[hebben]], so you say [[We zijn in 2018 getrouwd.]], 'we got married in 2018' — never [[Ik heb getrouwd]]. Many couples simply live together without marrying; that is [[samenwonen]], and the relationship itself is [[de relatie]]. Sadly, sometimes a marriage ends in a divorce, which is [[de scheiding]], and the verb is [[scheiden]]. You might gently say [[Mijn ouders zijn gescheiden.]], 'my parents are divorced.' A friendly question you will both ask and answer is [[Hoelang zijn jullie al getrouwd?]], which means 'how long have you been married?'. None of these words are difficult once you hear them a few times, so repeat each one after me, especially that tricky pair: [[We zijn getrouwd.]] with [[zijn]].

paragraphs.heading: Celebrations, congratulations & a little scene
paragraphs.text: Finally, celebrations. A birthday is [[de verjaardag]], and the Dutch take theirs seriously. At a typical Dutch party, the [[kringverjaardag]], everyone sits in a circle, drinks coffee and eats cake — it surprises many newcomers! When you arrive, you congratulate not only the birthday person but the whole family, saying [[Gefeliciteerd met je verjaardag!]], 'congratulations on your birthday!'. At a wedding you say [[Gefeliciteerd met jullie huwelijk!]] Now picture this real scene. Your neighbour shows you a photo. You smile and say [[Wat lijken jullie veel op elkaar!]] She answers [[Ja, dat is mijn broer.]] You ask [[Is hij getrouwd?]], and she says [[Ja, hij is vorig jaar getrouwd.]] You add warmly [[Wat leuk! Doe hem de groeten.]] See how all our pieces fit together — possessives like [[mijn]] and [[onze]], the verb [[lijken op]], visiting and marrying? You now have everything you need to chat about family in Dutch. So today, call a friend or a relative, describe the people in your family, say who you look like, and try one small phrase about a wedding or a visit. Do not worry about mistakes; every word you try makes the next one easier. [[Heel goed gedaan!]] Well done — I will see you in the next theme!
